claims.text: Adding a trace element with a significantly different atomic size increases lattice distortion in a high-entropy nanoalloy.
Increased lattice distortion promotes sluggish diffusion.
Sluggish diffusion enhances the structural and chemical stability of high-entropy nanoalloys at high temperature.
The proposed starting material is a near-equiatomic high-entropy nanoalloy with a homogeneous elemental distribution.
A controlled trace amount of a dopant with a markedly different atomic radius is introduced into the base alloy.
Dopant-induced lattice distortion produces a more disordered lattice structure.
Enhanced lattice distortion hinders atomic mobility.
Reduced atomic mobility lowers diffusion rates.
Lower diffusion rates minimize phase segregation under thermal stress.
Lower diffusion rates minimize grain growth under thermal stress.
After identical high-temperature exposure, the doped nanoalloy will have lower atomic diffusion rates than the undoped baseline.
After identical high-temperature exposure, the doped nanoalloy will exhibit less microstructural coarsening than the undoped baseline.
After identical high-temperature exposure, the doped nanoalloy will exhibit less chemical segregation than the undoped baseline.
The prediction is limited to nanoalloys with similar near-equiatomic compositions and to the tested high-temperature regime.
The predicted behavior may change when dopant concentration or temperature substantially exceeds the experimental limits.
The magnitude of diffusion reduction and stability enhancement may depend on dopant identity and concentration.
The effect on oxidation resistance under aggressive atmospheres is unknown.
Failure to observe a statistically significant diffusion reduction together with improved phase and chemical stability in the doped alloy would falsify the proposed mechanism.
